query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive model that explicitly incorporates microstructural defect effects—including randomly distributed point defects, grain boundary scattering, and trace oxygen impurities—will yield significantly more accurate electrical conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr than traditional analytical models based on perfect, defect‐free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy, processed via conventional methods, with a controlled impurity level (including a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen).
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a predictive approach (e.g., a machine‐learning–augmented or hybrid physics-informed model) that integrates microstructural defect information (such as oxygen-induced defect sites and scattering centers) into conductivity simulations.
generation.conditions: Two temperature regimes: a low-temperature regime (nearly 0–200 K) where defect-induced scattering may dominate electron mobility, and a high-temperature regime (300–1200 K) where thermal excitations activate additional conduction channels and defect dynamics. The approach is specifically applied to samples with up to 1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence and distribution of defects (e.g., vacancies, dislocations, and oxygen-associated sites) which alter the electron mean free paths compared to ideal crystals.
generation.mechanism: By incorporating the scattering effects and altered electronic structure due to defects and oxygen impurities, the model captures real microstructural influences on electron conduction. This leads to a more realistic description of both the low-temperature (carrier freeze-out or defect-scattering dominated) and high-temperature (thermally activated conduction and defect annealing/dynamics) conductivity mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: The enhanced predictive model will reduce the error in electrical conductivity predictions compared to defect‐free analytical approaches, with expected improvements (e.g., prediction error reduced from >20% to below ~10%) across both temperature regimes.
generation.baseline: Conventional analytical predictions based on ideal, perfect crystals that neglect the influence of microstructural defects and trace oxygen content.
generation.boundary: The model is applicable to bulk, polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr alloys under conditions where the oxygen impurity content does not exceed approximately 1 wt.% and may be limited to samples produced under controlled processing conditions; the temperature ranges are defined as 0–200 K for low-temperature behavior and 300–1200 K for high-temperature behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement (percentage error reduction) and sensitivity to variations in defect density or oxygen content are uncertain until comprehensive experimental validation is performed.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples using standard processing routes and prepare specimens with both nominally pure and 1 wt.% oxygen-doped conditions. Perform microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, atom probe tomography) to quantify defect types and densities. Then, measure the temperature-dependent electrical conductivity in two regimes: 0–200 K (low temperature) and 300–1200 K (high temperature). Compare the measured conductivity data with predictions from (a) the traditional analytical (defect-free) model and (b) the new predictive model that incorporates microstructural defects. Statistical analysis will determine if the new model significantly improves prediction accuracy.
measurements: Electrical conductivity as a function of temperature across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Microstructural defect density and type (via TEM, atom probe).
Oxygen content validation (e.g., via XPS or combustion analysis).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the new predictive model does not reduce the average prediction error by a statistically significant margin (e.g., failing to improve from >20% error to below ~10% error when compared to the conventional model) in either or both temperature regimes, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The Effect of Electronic Structure on the Phases Present in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractMulticomponent systems, termed High Entropy Alloys (HEAs), with predominantly single solid solution phases are a current area of focus in alloy development. Although different empirical rules have been introduced to understand phase formation and determine what the dominant phases may be in these systems, experimental investigation has revealed that in many cases their structure is not a single solid solution phase, and that the rules may not accurately distinguish the stability of the phase boundaries. Here, a combined modelling and experimental approach that looks into the electronic structure is proposed to improve accuracy of the predictions of the majority phase. To do this, the Rigid Band model is generalised for magnetic systems in prediction of the majority phase most likely to be found. Good agreement is found when the predictions are confronted with data from experiments, including a new magnetic HEA system (CoFeNiV). A comparison of explainable artificial intelligence methods in the phase classification of multi-principal element alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe demonstrate the capabilities of two model-agnostic local post-hoc model interpretability methods, namely breakDown (BD) and shapley (SHAP), to explain the predictions of a black-box classification learning model that establishes a quantitative relationship between chemical composition and multi-principal element alloys (MPEA) phase formation. We trained an ensemble of support vector machines using a dataset with 1,821 instances, 12 features with low pair-wise correlation, and seven phase labels. Feature contributions to the model prediction are computed by BD and SHAP for each composition. The resulting BD and SHAP transformed data are then used as inputs to identify similar composition groups using k-means clustering. Explanation-of-clusters by features reveal that the results from SHAP agree more closely with the literature. Visualization of compositions within a cluster using Ceteris-Paribus (CP) profile plots show the functional dependencies between the feature values and predicted response.
